text: You've built the model and run it through honest, purged validation. The last step is writing it up the way a hiring quant researcher actually wants to read it, and that write-up is its own skill, separate from the modeling work.

A reviewer isn't primarily grading whether your backtest made money. They're checking whether you avoided look-ahead bias, timestamping every feature and label to what was actually available at the time. They're checking whether you used proper purged and embargoed walk-forward validation instead of a random split that ignores time order. And they're checking whether you reported a skeptical, deflated performance estimate instead of one flattering number with no validation detail behind it, since trying multiple models without correcting for that is one of the most common mistakes a reviewer watches for.

A strong README walks through the problem, the data, the label you chose and why, the features you engineered, and then the validation plan, written as something decided before training, not reverse engineered from results you already liked. Results should appear as a distribution across folds, with the deflated Sharpe ratio noted if you tried more than one configuration, followed by an honest conclusion and what you'd test next.

Reporting one eye-catching Sharpe ratio without that detail is a red flag to anyone who has gotten this far in a course like this one. It signals either that the multiple-testing risk wasn't understood, or that it was understood and glossed over anyway, and either reading hurts your credibility more than a modest, carefully validated result would.

This course opened with a simple claim: finance is different, because signal to noise is low and the data keeps shifting underneath you. Every technique since then, careful labeling, purged validation, honest interpretation, skepticism toward any single flattering number, has been the practical response to that one claim. Tying your capstone write-up back to it shows a reviewer you understood the thesis, not just the individual tools. Course complete.
